provenance.other: “great and terrible” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses. Six attach it to something other than a day — a wilderness (Deuteronomy 1:19, 8:15), things done (10:21), God himself (Nehemiah 1:5, 4:14), a name (Psalm 99:3). Joel 2:31 is the only one that attaches it to a day, and Malachi 4:5, which the reader might expect, reads “the great and dreadful day of the LORD”.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 1:19 / Nehemiah 1:5, if the phrase is taken as a free-standing KJV intensifier rather than a citation.
provenance.significance: Recover Joel 2:31 and the borrowing acquires a date. “The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD come.” The narrator of 3 Nephi 4 uses that adjective pair four times in five verses of a battle in the nineteenth year, and four chapters later the sun really is darkened over the land for three days (3 Nephi 8). The book also closes its Malachi transcription at chapter 25 with the great and dreadful day itself. So the phrase is not merely lurid: it is the book quietly rehearsing, on a battlefield, the vocabulary of the day it is about to narrate.

4:7.note: “Great and terrible was the day that they did come up to battle… and great and terrible was the appearance of the armies of Giddianhi” — then again at 4:11 for the battle and the slaughter. The phrase is a KJV one and its distribution is the argument: of the seven verses that have it, only Joel 2:31 puts it on a day, and “great and terrible was the day” is what 3 Nephi 4:7 says. Below any quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion on the discrimination rather than on the run length. The 1830 text is unchanged here, and the fourfold repetition inside five verses is the narrator adopting the phrase rather than citing it once.
4:7.text: The sun shall be turned into darkness, and the moon into blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD come.

provenance.other: “dyed” occurs in exactly seven KJV verses; “skins dyed” occurs in exactly five, all of them the tabernacle’s covering of rams’ skins dyed red. The other two are Isaiah 63:1’s dyed garments from Bozrah and Ezekiel 23:15’s dyed attire.
provenance.significance: If the echo is real the effect is a vestment parody: the one thing the King James Bible dyes an animal skin for is the roof of the tabernacle, and the robbers come up to battle wearing lamb-skins dyed in blood. Isaiah 63:1-3, the other dyeing verse, would sharpen it further — the figure whose garments are red because he has trodden the winepress alone is the divine warrior, and here the red garments are on the army God is about to destroy.

4:7.note: “They had a lamb-skin about their loins, and they were dyed in blood.” Recorded as a gesture, not a case. The Book of Mormon’s only description of a dyed skin garment sits against a King James Bible whose only dyed skins are the rams’ skins dyed red of the tabernacle, and whose only other dyed cloth is Isaiah 63:1’s. No phrase is shared, so this is an echo at the level of a single collocation.
4:7.whyNot: There is no verbal contact beyond the word “dyed” and the presence of a skin, and “dyed in blood” is a natural description that needs no source. Exodus dyes rams’ skins red with a dye; the robbers are dyed in blood, which is not dyeing in the Exodus sense at all. A reader who declines this row is being reasonable, and the catalogue records it only so that the collocation is not silently passed over.
4:7.text: And rams’ skins dyed red, and badgers’ skins, and shittim wood,

provenance.other: “fallen to the earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, 2 Chronicles 20:24 and Acts 26:14. Acts has the closer four-word run (“all fallen to the earth”, against the Book of Mormon’s “had all fallen to the earth”), and is registered as an exclusion at this verse; the Chronicles verse has the whole chapter behind it.
provenance.alternative: Acts 26:14, on the four-word run alone.
provenance.significance: 2 Chronicles 20 is the King James Bible’s one full-dress narrative of a nation that wins a battle by not fighting it, and 3 Nephi 4 runs its whole sequence. Jehoshaphat’s people are outnumbered and besieged; they fast, gather to one place, and pray (20:4-13); the king and all Judah fall before the LORD (20:18); the LORD sets ambushments against the invaders (20:22); Judah comes to the watch tower and sees dead bodies fallen to the earth (20:24); they return to Jerusalem with singing and instruments (20:27-28); and God gives them rest round about (20:30). 3 Nephi 4 has every one of those beats in order — the gathering to one body (4:3), the prostration and cry (4:8), the ambush laid in the night that cuts off the retreat (4:24-25), the slaughter (4:11), the return to the place of security (4:15), and the breaking forth in singing and praising (4:31). The metaleptic gain is at the falling: 2 Chronicles 20 has two fallings, Judah falling before the LORD and the enemy fallen dead to the earth, and 3 Nephi 4 has exactly those two, in that order.

4:8.note: “The armies of the Nephites, when they saw the appearance of the army of Giddianhi, had all fallen to the earth, and did lift their cries to the Lord their God, that he would spare them, and deliver them out of the hands of their enemies.” The verbal foothold is thin — a four-word phrase the KJV uses twice — and it is offered as a foothold and nothing more. What carries the row is the shape. This is the Jehoshaphat type-scene, and the reason to catalogue it here rather than treat it as a commonplace is that the Book of Mormon reproduces the sequence and not merely the theme: prostration before the enemy, the Lord’s ambush, the dead on the field, the return, the song. Filed as figural precisely because the wording will not bear more than that; the confidence is on the sequence, not the words.
4:8.text: And when Judah came toward the watch tower in the wilderness, they looked unto the multitude, and, behold, they were dead bodies fallen to the earth, and none escaped.

provenance.route: Psalm 71:16 → KJV → Mosiah 9:17 → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “in the strength of the Lord” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Psalm 71:16 (“I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD”) and Micah 5:4 (“he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD”).
provenance.significance: The phrase entered the corpus at Mosiah 9:17 with the Psalm’s verb of motion attached — Zeniff goes forth to battle — and by 3 Nephi it has become a Nephite battle formula detached from either KJV verb. Its reappearance here, in the one chapter of 3 Nephi where an army stands still and receives a charge rather than making one, is the formula at its furthest remove from the Psalm that supplied it.

4:10.note: “In the strength of the Lord they did receive them.” Catalogued because a reader of 3 Nephi meets the phrase here for the first time in this book and should be told where it comes from, not because a fresh borrowing is being claimed: the discrimination that made Mosiah 9:17 a link — the Psalm’s “go” against Micah’s “stand and feed” — has nothing to bite on here, since the Nephite verb is “receive”. Recorded across the book boundary under ADJUDICATING §4, with the argument made at Mosiah 9:17 and not restated.
4:10.text: I will go in the strength of the Lord GOD: I will make mention of thy righteousness, even of thine only.

provenance.route: Luke 19:43 → KJV → Book of Mormon; Isaiah 29:3 fused in the same sentence
provenance.other: “in on every side” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 19:43, and the full clause “keep thee in on every side” occurs in exactly one KJV verse as well. “on every side” by itself occurs in thirty-two and is worthless; the discriminating word is the preposition that precedes it. The siege half of the sentence is Isaiah’s: “lay siege” occurs in exactly three KJV verses (Isaiah 29:3, Ezekiel 4:2, 4:3), and “camp against thee round about” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 29:3, which is the only one that also has the Book of Mormon’s “round about”.
provenance.significance: Both halves of this sentence are the King James Bible’s language for the siege of Jerusalem, and they come from its two ends. Isaiah 29:3 is the Lord besieging Ariel, the city where David dwelt; Luke 19:43-44 is Jesus weeping over the same city and telling it that its enemies will compass it round and keep it in on every side, “because thou knewest not the time of thy visitation.” 3 Nephi is the book of the visitation. Four chapters after this siege the Lord descends to the survivors at Bountiful, and the cities that are destroyed in 3 Nephi 8-9 are destroyed for exactly the reason Luke 19:44 gives. So the words in which Jesus dooms the city that missed its visitation are here used of the people who are about to receive theirs — and the outcome is inverted: Lachoneus’s people are hemmed in on every side and delivered.

4:16.note: “They came up on all sides to lay siege round about the people of Nephi… and should hem them in on every side.” Two KJV singletons inside one sentence, from the Bible’s two great siege oracles against Jerusalem. The Lukan phrase is the stronger of the two: four words, and “in on every side” is a preposition stack that occurs nowhere else in the King James Bible, so the agreement is not the common “on every side” but the awkward construction wrapped around it. Isaiah 29:3 supplies “lay siege” with “round about”, which no other KJV siege verse has together. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and not among his quotations; the case here is rarity, not length.
4:16.text: For the days shall come upon thee, that thine enemies shall cast a trench about thee, and compass thee round, and keep thee in on every side,

provenance.other: “perish with hunger” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 15:17, the prodigal son at the moment he comes to himself in a far country during a famine. The phrase is adjudicated at its first appearance in the volume, Mosiah 21:17.
provenance.significance: The parable’s hunger is what turns the prodigal round: he starves, comes to himself, and goes home to a father who receives him. 3 Nephi 4:20 puts that sentence on the robbers, and the chapters on either side follow the parable rather than the war. The hunger makes Zemnarihah’s people desire “to withdraw from their design” (4:22); many thousands then yield themselves up prisoners rather than die (4:27); and in the next chapter those of them who will covenant to keep the peace are not executed but “set at liberty” (3 Nephi 5:4-6). The one KJV verse in which starvation produces repentance is the verse the Book of Mormon reaches for at the point where starvation produces repentance.

4:20.note: “The wild game became scarce in the wilderness, insomuch that the robbers were about to perish with hunger.” A KJV singleton, and its second use in the corpus after Mosiah 21:17 — recorded here as a fresh link because the book is new and the reader page is per-book (ADJUDICATING §4), and because the use is different: Mosiah has a relief measure to keep widows from perishing, 3 Nephi has an enemy army starving toward surrender. Below Skousen’s threshold and not among his quotations.
4:20.text: And when he came to himself, he said, How many hired servants of my father’s have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!

provenance.other: “by day and by night” — with the preposition repeated — occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Isaiah 28:19. The King James Bible has “day and night” everywhere and the doubled preposition only here. The Book of Mormon has the construction twice, at 3 Nephi 4:21 and, reversed, at 4:22.
provenance.significance: Isaiah 28:15-19 is the covenant with death and the overflowing scourge: “when the overflowing scourge shall pass through, then ye shall be trodden down by it… morning by morning shall it pass over, by day and by night.” What Isaiah describes is not a battle but an unresting, repeated passing-over that wears a people out, and that is exactly the Nephite tactic 4:21 describes — continual sorties, not a set engagement, until 4:22 reports the effect in Isaiah’s own terms, “the great destruction which come upon them by night and by day.” The Book of Mormon has taken the scourge oracle’s picture of relentlessness and given it to the side it approves of.

4:21.note: “The Nephites were continually marching out by day and by night, and falling upon their armies, and cutting them off by thousands and by tens of thousands.” The doubled preposition is the whole of the verbal evidence and it is enough to name a source, because the KJV writes it that way once. Held at moderate rather than high: four words is little, the sense of Isaiah’s clause is temporal where the Book of Mormon’s is adverbial, and a writer with the KJV in his ear could produce the doubling unprompted. The reversal at 4:22 is what tips it — the phrase is being handled, not merely used.
4:21.text: From the time that it goeth forth it shall take you: for morning by morning shall it pass over, by day and by night: and it shall be a vexation only to understand the report.

provenance.other: “hanged on a tree” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Joshua 8:29, Esther 2:23, Acts 5:30, Acts 10:39 — and Deuteronomy 21:22 and Galatians 3:13 give the same idiom in other grammatical forms. The Book of Mormon reads “hanged upon a tree”, with a preposition no King James verse uses of this act. Of the four, only Joshua 8:29 hangs the defeated commander of an army after a battle won by an ambush, and only Joshua 8:29 and 10:26-27 have the body brought down and a monument made of the site.
provenance.alternative: Deuteronomy 21:22-23 as the law behind the act, mediated by Galatians 3:13 (“Cursed is every one that hangeth on a tree”). tools/mediation-check.py returns no decisive divergence between the Deuteronomy and Galatians forms, because the Book of Mormon reproduces no clause that the two of them word differently; the mediation cannot be settled from this verse.
provenance.significance: The end of the robbers is the fall of Ai. Joshua 8 is a battle won by a force that marches out in the night and places itself beyond the city so that the enemy is caught between two armies — “so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side” (8:22) — and it ends with the king of Ai hanged on a tree and the site marked. 3 Nephi 4:24-25 has Gidgiddoni send his armies out in the night-time to get beyond the robbers and cut off the way of their retreat, so that on the morrow they are met “both in their front and in their rear”; 4:26 accounts for the ones on the south; and 4:28 hangs the leader on a tree. Read against Joshua 8, the felling of the tree at 4:28-29 is the Book of Mormon supplying the monument the Hebrew narrative supplies with a heap of stones, and Deuteronomy 21:23’s requirement that the body not remain on the tree is satisfied by bringing the tree down rather than the man.

4:28.note: “Their leader, Zemnarihah, was taken, and hanged upon a tree, yea, even upon the top thereof, until he was dead.” The idiom is the King James Bible’s and the narrative is Joshua’s. What makes this more than a commonplace is that the two preceding verses have already run Joshua 8’s tactics: a night march to a position beyond the enemy, the enemy met front and rear on the morrow, the survivors cut off in their places of retreat. The execution then lands where Joshua 8 lands. Note the departure that is not KJV: the Book of Mormon writes “upon a tree”, which no King James verse does of a hanging, and adds “even upon the top thereof”, a detail no biblical hanging has — “top thereof” occurs in exactly two KJV verses and neither is a gallows. The borrowing is of an act and its idiom, not of a clause, which is why this is filed as an allusion and not a quotation.
4:28.text: And the king of Ai he hanged on a tree until eventide: and as soon as the sun was down, Joshua commanded that they should take his carcase down from the tree, and cast it at the entering of the gate of the city, and raise thereon a great heap of stones, that remaineth unto this day.

provenance.other: “hew down” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 12:3 (graven images) and Daniel 4:14 (the tree). Matthew 3:10 and Luke 3:9 have “hewn down” of the fruitless tree at the root of which the axe is laid.
provenance.significance: Daniel 4 is the King James Bible’s one narrative in which a felled tree IS a deposed ruler: “Hew down the tree… It is thou, O king” (4:14, 4:22). 3 Nephi 4:28-29 makes the same identification explicitly and in the opposite direction — the ruler is put on the tree, the tree is brought down with him on it, and the crowd then reads the act as a sign, praying that all who seek to slay them may be “fell to the earth, even as this man hath been fell to the earth.” The tree and the man are made one thing by the ritual rather than by a dream.

4:29.note: “That they may cause to be fell to the earth all who shall seek to slay them because of power and secret combinations, even as this man hath been fell to the earth.” Recorded as a gesture toward Daniel 4, not as a demonstrated borrowing: the Book of Mormon’s felling is a real tree brought down over a real corpse, and Daniel’s is a vision, but Daniel 4 is the only place in the King James Bible where cutting down a tree is the deposing of a man, and 3 Nephi 4:29 is a chant that says exactly that. The 1830 text is evidence here — it reads the causative “fell the tree to the earth” and “cause to be fell”, twice, which 1920 regularised to “felled”; the first edition’s odd verb is what makes the felling read as a performed sentence rather than a tidying of the battlefield.
4:29.whyNot: There is no shared wording at all. “Hew down the tree” and “fall the tree to the earth” have the tree in common and nothing else, and a people who have just hanged a man on a tree have an obvious reason to cut the tree down that requires no source. A reader who takes this as ordinary reprisal and not as an allusion has the better of the evidence; it is here because the identification of tree with ruler is unusual enough to be worth pointing at.
4:29.text: He cried aloud, and said thus, Hew down the tree, and cut off his branches, shake off his leaves, and scatter his fruit: let the beasts get away from under it, and the fowls from his branches:

provenance.route: Exodus 3:6/3:15 → New Testament → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 22:32, Mark 12:26, Luke 20:37, Acts 7:32 — and all four are New Testament. Exodus never writes it that way: 3:6, 3:15 and 4:5 all read “the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob”, without the conjunction before Isaac, and 3:16 compresses further to “the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob”.
provenance.alternative: Exodus 3:15, which is the formula’s home and which the Book of Mormon does not follow.
provenance.significance: The decisive metalepsis is Matthew’s next clause. In the Gospels this formula is not a doxology but a proof text: Jesus quotes it to the Sadducees and immediately draws the inference, “God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.” The Nephites cry it standing on a field where the slaughter has been the greatest ever known among the people of Lehi (4:11), over an enemy leader they have just hanged. The one thing the New Testament does with these words is argue from them that the dead are not dead, and the Book of Mormon puts them in the mouths of survivors counting corpses, four chapters before the resurrected Christ appears to them.

4:30.note: “May the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, protect this people in righteousness.” Fourteen words reproduced exactly, and the mediation turns on a single conjunction, as it did at 1 Nephi 6:4 and Alma 36:2. tools/mediation-check.py cannot settle it — run against Exodus 3:15 and Matthew 22:32 it reports no decisive divergence, because it ignores single common words and “and” is the only word at which the two forms differ (ADJUDICATING §4 leaves that class to the eye). By eye the answer is unambiguous: every Old Testament occurrence omits the conjunction before Isaac and every New Testament occurrence has it, and the Book of Mormon has it. Below Skousen’s sixteen-word threshold and not among his thirty-six; on run length this is nonetheless the longest continuous KJV agreement in the chapter.
4:30.text: I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob? God is not the God of the dead, but of the living.

provenance.other: “were as one” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 5:13, where the trumpeters and singers were as one in praising and thanking the LORD. “break forth into singing” occurs in exactly four KJV verses, all Isaiah — 14:7, 44:23, 49:13, 54:1.
provenance.significance: Both halves of the sentence look forward inside this book. 2 Chronicles 5:13 is the dedication of Solomon’s temple, and what happens the moment the congregation is as one in praising is that the house is filled with a cloud and the glory of the Lord; 3 Nephi 11 is a congregation gathered at a temple to whom the Lord in fact descends. Isaiah 54:1, the fourth of the “break forth into singing” verses, is transcribed entire seventeen chapters later as 3 Nephi 22:1, out of the mouth of the risen Christ. So a victory chant on a battlefield is made of the KJV’s language for the moment a temple is filled and for the song the book’s Christ will hand back to this people as a prophecy.

4:31.note: “They did break forth, all as one, in singing and praising their God, for the great thing which he had done for them.” Two KJV phrases fused, neither reproduced whole: the Book of Mormon has “all as one” against the King James “were as one”, and it splits “break forth into singing” by putting “all as one” inside it. The 2 Chronicles verse carries more weight than the count alone suggests, because it supplies not only the singleton but the two verbs the Book of Mormon pairs — “praising and thanking” against “singing and praising”. Held at moderate: neither phrase is reproduced exactly, and a congregation praising in unison is not a rare thing to describe.
4:31.text: It came even to pass, as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the LORD; and when they lifted up their voice with the trumpets and cymbals and instruments of musick, and praised the LORD, saying, For he is good; for his mercy endureth for ever: that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the LORD;

provenance.other: “Hosanna” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Matthew 21:9, 21:15, Mark 11:9, 11:10, John 12:13 — and all five belong to the triumphal entry. The word is absent from the Old Testament entirely. “Hosanna to the” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, both in Matthew 21, and both read “Hosanna to the son of David”.
provenance.significance: Matthew’s acclamation is a tricolon: Hosanna to the son of David — Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord — Hosanna in the highest. 3 Nephi 4:32 is the same three beats with the middle term altered: Hosanna to the Most High God — Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty — the Most High God. Even Matthew’s closing “in the highest” is answered, by the repetition of “the Most High”. What the crowd shouts at the gate of Jerusalem to a king riding in, the Nephites shout on a battlefield in the twenty-first year; and 3 Nephi 11:17 will have a multitude cry Hosanna again, this time with the person Matthew’s crowd was greeting standing in front of them.

4:32.note: “Yea, they did cry, Hosanna to the Most High God; and they did cry, Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty, the Most High God.” Hosanna is a New Testament word in the King James Bible and only ever a triumphal-entry word, so its appearance in a Nephite war-cry dated to the first century BC is an anachronism of the plainest kind — the second in the volume after 1 Nephi 11:6, and the first put in a crowd’s mouth. The structure is the argument as much as the word: “Hosanna to the …” is Matthew’s construction, and the acclamation that follows keeps Matthew’s order of blessing and superlative.
4:32.text: And the multitudes that went before, and that followed, cried, saying, Hosanna to the son of David: Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord; Hosanna in the highest.

provenance.other: “Lord God Almighty” occurs in exactly five KJV verses — Revelation 4:8, 11:17, 15:3, 16:7, 21:22 — and every one of them is in the Revelation of John. The Old Testament has “God Almighty” (Genesis 28:3 and four others) but never with “Lord” before it.
provenance.significance: The title is the one 1 Nephi 1:14 borrowed at the head of the volume, from the verse that identifies the words Lehi sings as “the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”. Its return here puts the same Apocalypse vocabulary on the other end of the book, and in the same breath as Hosanna: a Nephite army praises God in a doxology whose two halves come from the Gospels’ account of Palm Sunday and from John’s vision of the saints singing beside the sea of glass. Both are victory songs sung to a deliverer who has not yet appeared, which is what 3 Nephi 4 is.

4:32.note: “Blessed be the name of the Lord God Almighty, the Most High God.” Recorded across the book boundary; the argument for the title’s KJV specificity was made at 1 Nephi 1:14 and is not restated. What is new here is the pairing. The verse sets a title the King James Bible uses only in Revelation beside a word the King James Bible uses only at the triumphal entry, and gives both to a crowd on a battlefield — so the doxology has no Old Testament vocabulary in it at all, in a chapter narrated as first-century-BC history. Filed as an echo rather than an allusion because only the title is shared and none of Revelation 15:3’s surrounding clauses.
4:32.text: And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.

provenance.other: “delivered them out of the hands” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Judges 8:34, which continues “of all their enemies on every side”. The King James Bible’s ordinary idiom is the singular, “out of the hand of”; the plural “hands” with “their enemies” is Judges 8:34’s alone. The machine proposed Judges 2:14 for the same words and it is registered as an exclusion — 2:14 delivers Israel INTO the hands of enemies, which is the opposite transaction.
provenance.significance: Judges 8:34 is not a deliverance verse. It is the verse that records the forgetting of one: “And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side.” 3 Nephi 4:33 is the exact photographic negative — the people know why they were delivered, name it as their repentance and their humility, and weep. The negative does not hold for long. Within two chapters the same people are dividing into classes, “lifted up unto pride and boastings because of their exceeding great riches” (3 Nephi 6:10-15), which is what Judges 8:34 describes happening to Israel after Gideon. The catalogue’s reading is that the borrowed clause is doing the work of a warning the narrator has not yet made explicit.

4:33.note: “Because of the great goodness of God in delivering them out of the hands of their enemies; and they knew it was because of their repentance and their humility that they had been delivered from an everlasting destruction.” The five-word run is a KJV singleton, and the same clause is used at 4:8 as a petition before the battle — “deliver them out of the hands of their enemies” — so the chapter opens and closes on it. Held at moderate rather than high because the phrase is close to the KJV’s common deliverance idiom and the plural could be inadvertent; what recommends the identification is that the plural is Judges’, and Judges is the book whose whole shape is deliverance followed by forgetting.
4:33.text: And the children of Israel remembered not the LORD their God, who had delivered them out of the hands of all their enemies on every side:

provenance.other: “everlasting destruction” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Thessalonians 1:9. The phrase is adjudicated in the corpus at Helaman 8:26 and recurs across nine Book of Mormon verses.
provenance.significance: 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9 is a coming: “the Lord Jesus shall be revealed from heaven with his mighty angels, in flaming fire taking vengeance on them that know not God… who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord.” That paragraph is the programme of the next five chapters of 3 Nephi. Four chapters after this verse the cities burn, the earth is broken up, and a voice from heaven tells the survivors which cities were destroyed and why (3 Nephi 8-9); then the Lord is revealed from heaven and the survivors who were spared are the ones who fall at his feet. The chapter’s last word is the New Testament’s one word for the fate everyone else meets, and the Book of Mormon puts it on the people who escape it.

4:33.note: “They knew it was because of their repentance and their humility that they had been delivered from an everlasting destruction.” A two-word borrowing from a KJV singleton, filed as an echo for the same reason it was at Helaman 8:26: the phrase is short enough that a preacher’s ear could produce it and nothing else of 2 Thessalonians 1 is present in the sentence. It is recorded again here, across the book boundary, because the Pauline context bears on 3 Nephi in a way it did not bear on Helaman — the paragraph the phrase comes from describes a revelation from heaven in flaming fire, and 3 Nephi is the book that narrates one.
4:33.text: Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;
